title: Why "Work Harder" is a Terrible Plan
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart challenges the common student goal-setting default of "I'll just work harder," arguing it's a vague, unmeasurable plan that reliably produces anxiety and lower self-confidence rather than results. Drawing on the lead-indicator/lag-indicator framework from The 4 Disciplines of Execution, he explains that "improve my grades" is a lag indicator -- a final measurement you only see once it's too late to act -- while genuinely useful goals require lead indicators: specific, trackable actions like a set number of weekly self-quizzes or PowerSchool checks. He walks through concrete examples of converting "work harder" into measurable weekly actions, arguing that most students would benefit far more from clarity about what hard work looks like than from raw effort. The piece is a practical, classroom-tested rebuttal to well-meaning but useless goal-setting advice.
points: Stuart's core diagnosis: "work harder" fails as a goal because it can't be measured mid-course, so students can't tell whether they're on track until it's too late.
He imports the lead-indicator/lag-indicator distinction from The 4 Disciplines of Execution directly into classroom goal-setting, giving teachers a transferable framework beyond this one example.
His concrete goal rewrites (e.g., "2x per week, quiz myself with the study guide for 25 minutes") model exactly how to convert vague effort language into trackable weekly actions.
He explicitly links "work harder" as a plan to increased student anxiety and decreased self-confidence, based on years of observing the pattern play out.
quotes: Working harder," I tell them, "is a terrific recipe for being anxious and getting down on yourself. I'm not sharing this with you as my opinion. I'm sharing this with you as someone who has seen hundreds and hundreds of students decide that what they'll do to improve themselves is 'work harder.'
If I set my goal to "improve my grades" by the end of the month by "working harder," how am I going to measure, in the midst of working toward that goal, whether or not I am on the path?

A lag indicator is a final measurement of success. Student achievement scores are a perfect (and terrible) example. They are lag indicators because you get these measurements once the work is done, once the verdict is in.

2x per week, I'm going to quiz myself with the study guide for 25 minutes. 5x per week, I'm going to check my class progress on PowerSchool and see whether I'm turning my assignments in; when I've missed one, I'm going to figure out how to make that right.
Though many of my students could very well benefit from working harder, they'll benefit much more from being clear on what hard work looks like and finding ways to measure and keep track of that.
